subtitle.en: Four hunters you can see from almost any road

intro.en:
Birds of prey seem difficult: they are often far away, and they are usually in the air. But you don't need to see every feather. Look at shape and behaviour: the way it flies is half the identification.

Britain's birds of prey have had an extraordinary comeback. The Red Kite was almost extinct, down to a few pairs in Wales. Today you can see one from the motorway in the Chilterns. In this lesson we meet four of the ones you are most likely to see: one circling, one hovering, one flashing through a garden, and one forked-tailed glider.

At the end there's a quiz of eight questions, with two birds from last week mixed in.

explain.en: A dark patch on the underside of the wing, at the bend.
A bill with a sharp hook at the tip, for tearing meat.
A bare patch of skin, often yellow, at the top of the bill, where the nostrils are.

look_for.en: In flight: dark **wrist patch** under the wing

where_when.en: Over woods and fields, soaring in circles, or sitting on a post or a pylon. The commonest bird of prey in Britain, especially in the west.

describe.en: A far-carrying, mewing "pee-ow", often given high up in the sky.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: They vary a lot, from almost white to nearly black. The shape does not.

look_for.en: Hovers: hangs in the air with fluttering wings
Grey head, chestnut back with black spots
Grey tail with a black band near the tip

where_when.en: Roadside verges, fields and motorways. Hovers over the grass, looking for voles. Sits on poles and wires.

describe.en: A shrill, quick "kee-kee-kee-kee", usually near the nest.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: The female has a brown, barred tail, and a brown head.

look_for.en: Short, rounded wings and a long tail

where_when.en: Woods, hedges and gardens. Flies low and fast, then bursts out from behind a hedge to catch a small bird. You often see a flash, then a puff of feathers.

describe.en: A fast, chattering "kek-kek-kek-kek", usually only heard near the nest.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

dont_confuse.en: Kestrel (just before): longer, pointed wings, and a habit of hovering.

look_for.en: Rusty-red body, with a pale grey head
Long, deeply forked tail, twisting as it steers
Long wings, with white patches under the tips

where_when.en: Open countryside in the Chilterns, Wales, central Scotland, Yorkshire and the east Midlands, soaring slowly and gliding low over fields. Often seen over villages and roads, and at feeding stations.

describe.en: A thin, mewing "weeoo-weeoo-weeoo", higher and thinner than a Buzzard.

sound.status: chosen on xeno-canto details; listen before use

note.en: Red Kites were reintroduced to England and Scotland from 1989, with birds from Spain and Sweden.

text.en: Look at the tail and the wings. A Red Kite has a long, forked tail that it twists as it steers, and long, narrow wings with a bend. A Buzzard has a short, rounded tail and broader wings, held in a shallow V when it soars.

outside.en: Watch the sky next time you are on a car trip or walk. Is the bird soaring in circles (Buzzard), hovering (Kestrel) or twisting its forked tail (Red Kite)? Write down what the bird did, not just what it looked like.
